Bonafide F1 Predictions 2025

Sawyer Stein

This chart shows the average accuracy for each type of prediction. Some types of predictions appear easier to get right than others.

This chart shows how often each type of prediction was actually used in the dataset. Some prediction types appear much more frequently than others.

Displays of Confidence Intervals:

This plot shows the average accuracy for each type of prediction along with a range showing uncertainty around the estimate. The dashed line at 50% represents the accuracy someone would expect if they were guessing randomly.

This heatmap shows prediction accuracy using colors. Green areas represent higher accuracy, while red areas represent lower accuracy. This makes it easy to quickly see which prediction types performed better or worse.

## # A tibble: 2 × 3
##   Group  mean_acc     n
##   <chr>     <dbl> <int>
## 1 Driver    0.484    62
## 2 Team      0.769    13
## 
##  2-sample test for equality of proportions with continuity correction
## 
## data:  tapply(combined$Accuracy, combined$Group, sum) out of tapply(combined$Accuracy, combined$Group, length)
## X-squared = 2.463, df = 1, p-value = 0.1166
## alternative hypothesis: two.sided
## 95 percent confidence interval:
##  -0.59251719  0.02179759
## sample estimates:
##    prop 1    prop 2 
## 0.4838710 0.7692308

This test checks whether the difference between driver prediction accuracy and team prediction accuracy is large enough to be meaningful. The results suggest the difference could easily happen by chance, so we cannot confidently say one type is better than the other.

This chart compares how often predictions about drivers were correct versus how often predictions about teams were correct. Team predictions were correct slightly more often, but the difference is small.

##   n_drivers

##  Pearson's Chi-squared test
## 
## data:  driver_table2
## X-squared = 3.2031, df = 7, p-value = 0.8656

This test checks whether some drivers are predicted correctly more often than others. The results show no clear evidence that the specific driver affects prediction accuracy.

##    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
##   1.469   1.531   2.490   3.062   4.454   6.122
## Analysis of Deviance Table
## 
## Model: binomial, link: logit
## 
## Response: Accuracy
## 
## Terms added sequentially (first to last)
## 
## 
##        Df Deviance Resid. Df Resid. Dev Pr(>Chi)
## NULL                      48     67.908         
## Driver  7   3.2605        41     64.648   0.8599

This model looks at whether knowing which driver was predicted helps explain whether the prediction was correct. The results suggest that the driver alone does not strongly explain prediction accuracy.

##                          Factor    p-value                          Conclusion
## 1            Which driver it is 0.85990840        No clear evidence it matters
## 2 What kind of prediction it is 0.02990349 Matters (statistically significant)

This model checks whether the type of prediction helps explain whether the prediction was correct. The results suggest that prediction type may matter more than the driver being predicted.

## Summary (controlling for both factors):
## - Which driver it is:does NOT show clear evidence of mattering. (p =0.86)
## - What kind of prediction it is:matters. (p =0.03)
## 
## Interpretation:
## Accuracy differences are driven more by the TYPE of prediction than by the specific driver.

Plot of Info:

Prediction accuracy varies more by prediction type than by driver. Predictions that a driver will not win are highly accurate, likely because race wins are rare events. In contrast, season-level predictions are the least accurate, suggesting that long-term performance is more difficult to forecast than race-level outcomes.

Is L-Bone a Lando Jinx?

## # A tibble: 2 × 4
##   pred_norris total_predictions correct_predictions accuracy_rate
##   <lgl>                   <int>               <int>         <dbl>
## 1 FALSE                       9                   1         0.111
## 2 TRUE                        6                   2         0.333
##        
##         FALSE TRUE
##   FALSE     8    1
##   TRUE      4    2
## 
##  Fisher's Exact Test for Count Data
## 
## data:  tab
## p-value = 0.956
## alternative hypothesis: true odds ratio is less than 1
## 95 percent confidence interval:
##    0.0000 129.8356
## sample estimates:
## odds ratio 
##   3.622029

This test checks whether predictions involving Lando Norris were more likely to be wrong. The results show no evidence that predicting Norris leads to worse results.

## [1] 0.9557

This plot shows what the difference in prediction accuracy would look like if there were no real effect from picking Norris. The bars show results from many random re-shuffles of the data. The vertical line shows the actual difference we observed in the real predictions. Because the line falls well within the range of the random results, it suggests the difference could easily happen by chance. In simple terms, the plot supports the idea that picking Norris does not meaningfully change prediction accuracy.
